The source systematic review and meta-analysis was designed to compare the clinical effectiveness of operative with nonoperative treatment for displaced midshaft clavicular fractures (DMCF).

The authors systematically searched electronic databases (MEDILINE, EMBASE, CLINICAL, OVID, BIOSIS and Cochrane registry of controlled clinical trials) to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in which operative treatment was compared with nonoperative treatment for DMCF from 1980 to 2012.
Four RCTs with a total of 321 patients were screened for the present study.

Results showed that the operative treatment was superior to the nonoperative treatment regarding the rate of nonunion [95 % confidence interval (CI) (0.05, 0.43), P = 0.0004], malunion [95 % CI (0.06, 0.34), P < 0.00001] and overall complication [95 % CI (0.43-0.76), P = 0.0001].

Subgroup analyses of complications revealed that significant differences were existed in the incidence of neurologic symptoms [95 % CI (0.20, 0.74), P = 0.004] and dissatisfaction with appearance [95 % CI (0.19, 0.65), P = 0.001].
Lack of consistent and standardized assessment data, insufficiency analysis that carried out showed improved functional outcomes (P < 0.05) in operative treatment.

The reported improvement in functional outcomes with operative treatment was derived from an analysis carried out in the setting of a lack of consistent and standardized assessment data, so that functional-outcome result rests on incomplete and non-standardized assessment.

The first prototype of the sternal skin conductance device was not able to collect any analyzable skin conductance data because of malfunction issues including poor conductance and battery failure, so it produced no hot flash measurements to compare with women's reports.

The device-based hot flash findings came from three small descriptive pilot studies using two sequential prototypes, worn either in a monitored setting for 24 hours or in an ambulatory setting for 5 weeks; such a descriptive pilot design cannot establish diagnostic validity of the device against a reference standard.

In a separate prospective study of 56 women recently treated for breast cancer who completed a 14-day Hot Flashes and Anxiety Diary, hot flashes were objectively recorded for a continuous 24-hour period using home-based sternal skin conductance; greater anxiety on the diary was significantly associated with a shorter time to reach the hot flash peak as assessed with sternal skin conductance (partial Spearman correlation coefficient rsp = -0.44).

Acceptability was reported by 16 women who wore the sternal skin conductance device for 5 weeks, who reported that wearing the device was acceptable, although 31% stated that it interfered with daily activities.

The device was worn either in a monitored setting for 24 hours or in an ambulatory setting for 5 weeks, and during the study period women recorded hot flashes in a prospective hot flash diary and answered questions about the acceptability of wearing the device.

Yes — in a retrospective series of 425 consecutive patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma treated between January 2006 and December 2008, preoperative platelet count was an independent prognostic factor on multivariate analysis (P = 0.013), together with T grade (P = 0.017) and N staging (P < 0.001).

A receiver operating characteristic curve for survival prediction was plotted to verify the optimum cutoff point for preoperative platelet count, which was 205 × 10(9)/L; univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to evaluate prognostic parameters.
Yes: the Disposable Antibacterial Coating (DAC) hydrogel combined with various antibacterial compounds showed both a bactericidal and an antibiofilm effect in vitro.

In that in vitro work, antibacterial activity was determined by broth microdilution and antibiofilm activity by a crystal violet assay, and complete release of all tested antibacterial compounds from the hydrogel was observed in less than 96 hours.
The ability of the DAC hydrogel to deliver antibacterial agents was tested using spectrophotometry and a microbiologic assay.
Coating resistance to press-fit insertion was tested in rabbit tibias and human femurs, and approximately 80% of the hydrogel coating was retrieved on the implant after press-fit insertion.

Yes — determination of specific IgE against components with ISAC 112 was reported as a reproducible technique, with very good intra- and inter-assay agreement for 94 allergens and good agreement for one.

Reliability of the ISAC 112 technique was studied intra- and inter-assay and inter-batch- and inter-laboratory-assay in 20 samples consisting of 19 sera from polysensitized allergic patients plus the manufacturer's calibrator (CTR02); CTR02 and three patients' sera were measured ten times in the same and in different assays, and all samples were tested in two laboratories and with two batches of ISAC kit.

Precision was assessed by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the 15 allergens generating the calibration curve, while repeatability and reproducibility were assessed by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) calculated for each allergen.
In the inter-batch analysis, very good agreement was obtained for 82 allergens, good for 14, moderate for 5, poor for 1 and bad for 1 allergen.
In the inter-laboratory analysis, very good agreement was obtained for 73 allergens, good for 22, moderate for 6 and poor for 2 allergens.
The mean CV obtained in the CTR02 determinations was 9.4%, while the variability of the patients' sera was 22.9%.

Yes — in the cited single series of postoperative cerebrospinal fluid fistulas after spine surgery, the ten patients treated with an external lumbar CSF drain for ten days were cured in a mean of 10 days versus a mean of 30 days for the six patients treated conservatively, and all patients healed their wound properly with no adverse events recorded.
Postoperative CSF fistulas were described in 16 of 198 patients (8%) who underwent spine surgery between 2009 and 2010, and the mean follow-up period was ten months.
Six of these patients were treated conservatively by positioning prone for three weeks, while ten were treated by placing an external CSF lumbar drainage for ten days.

The therapeutic strategy was chosen according to the patients' clinical condition, including the feasibility of continuous prone positioning and the morbidity risk of prolonged bed rest, so the reported healing times come from a non-randomized comparison in which the faster healing in the drained group cannot be attributed to lumbar drainage alone.

HFNC were not noisier than bubble CPAP in preterm infants: there was no evidence of a difference in average noise levels measured at the external auditory meatus, with a mean difference (95% CI) of -1.6 (-4.0 to 0.9) dBA for HFNC compared to BCPAP.
At low frequency (500 Hz), HFNC was mean (95% CI) 3.0 (0.3 to 5.7) dBA quieter than BCPAP.

These findings come from an observational study of preterm infants receiving HFNC or BCPAP in which noise within the external auditory meatus was measured with a microphone probe tube connected to a calibrated digital dosimeter across a range of frequencies and reported as dBA; 21 HFNC and 13 BCPAP noise measurements were performed in 21 infants, with HFNC gas flows of 2-5 L/min and BCPAP gas flows of 6-10 L/min at set pressures of 5-7 cm of water.

No: in a retrospective cohort of 151 women with bothersome mixed urinary incontinence, concomitant anterior/apical (AA) repair added to a midurethral sling (MUS) did not improve the overactive bladder component, with a 6-week OAB-q Symptom Severity (OAB-q SS) change score of 30 ± 26 for MUS-only versus 25 ± 25 for MUS + AA (p = 0.20), indicating similar improvements in OAB symptoms in both groups.
Of the 151 women in the cohort, 67 (44%) underwent MUS-only and 84 (56%) underwent MUS + AA; the MUS-only group was younger and had less severe baseline prolapse (p < 0.05 for both).

Multivariate linear regression analysis also revealed no difference in OAB-q SS change score between the MUS-only and MUS + AA cohorts, although change scores were lower among women who had a postoperative complication (β = -19, 95% CI -31 to -6; p < 0.01).

Across all subjects, mean OAB-q SS scores improved significantly after surgery (p < 0.05), so the improvement in overactive bladder symptoms was attributable to surgery overall rather than to the addition of anterior/apical repair.

In a prospective pilot study of 23 consecutive patients (12 male, 11 female) with a stage III or stages III and IV osteochondritis dissecans lesion (mostly stage III) who were admitted for surgery, a distinct serum vitamin D3 deficiency was found in the majority (18/23), two patients were vitamin D3-insufficient, and in three patients the vitamin D3 level reached the lowest normal value.

HIF1A is characterized in the study as a major vascular epithelial growth factor regulator under hypoxic conditions, and the study enrolled 87 AMD patients and 80 healthy subjects at the Department of Ophthalmology, Pamukkale University Hospital, Denizli, Turkey, of whom 45 (52%) had wet-type AMD and 42 (48%) had dry-type AMD.

In that case-control analysis, both rs11549465 and rs11549467 (HIF1A) were investigated in DNA isolated from peripheral blood samples of cases and controls by dye-termination DNA sequencing, and no statistically significant difference in the distributions of the HIF1A single nucleotide polymorphisms emerged between patients and healthy subjects; the only significant genetic association reported in this cohort was for CFH rs1061170, where having at least one C allele increased AMD risk independent of age (OR = 2.42, 95% CI 1.22-4.81).

Yes, in a retrospective case-control study, anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) failure was associated with steeper medial and lateral posterior tibial slopes (PTS): the odds ratio of ACLR failure was 6.8 for medial PTS >= 5 degrees (P = 0.007) and 10.8 for lateral PTS >= 5 degrees (P = 0.000).

The study comprised 20 ACLR failure cases and 20 randomly selected controls, drawn from 238 eligible patients identified between June 2009 and October 2010, and reported an overall ACLR failure rate of 8.4%.

The medial PTS of the ACLR failure group was reported as significantly steeper than that of the control group, with values of 3.5 degrees +/- 2.5 degrees versus 6.1 degrees +/- 2.1 degrees (P = 0.000).
The lateral PTS of the ACLR failure group was likewise reported as significantly steeper than that of the control group, at 2.9 degrees +/- 2.1 degrees versus 5.5 degrees +/- 3.0 degrees (P = 0.006).

Medial and lateral PTS were measured on magnetic resonance imaging scans using Hudek's measurement method; across all 40 participants the mean medial PTS was 4.1 degrees +/- 3.2 degrees and the mean lateral PTS was 4.6 degrees +/- 2.6 degrees.

Because these findings come from a retrospective case-control comparison of PTS between failure and control groups, the design supports an association between steeper PTS and ACLR failure but cannot establish that modifying or lowering PTS prevents graft failure.

The purposes of this study were to report the alveolar process thickness and inter-radicular space in the posterior region of the mandible, to assess the impact of different miniscrew insertion angle protocols, and to identify differences between the genders or types of malocclusion.
The primary outcome variables were bone thickness and inter-radicular space.

The inter-radicular spaces were evaluated 5 mm from the cement-enamel junction, and the bone thicknesses were taken at 45°, 60°, and 90° in relation to the alveolar ridge, simulating a miniscrew insertion.
In this retrospective study, 100 individuals were selected for orthodontic treatment at a radiology clinic; cone-beam computed tomography data were imported into 3-dimensional software.
The sample was composed of 100 patients with a mean age of 17.4 ± 6.74 years; there were 61 female and 39 male patients and 60 Class I and 40 Class II molar relationships.
The inter-radicular space ranged from 2.46 to 3.31 mm, and alveolar bone thickness ranged from 8.01 to 13.77 mm.
The thickness tended to decrease with the increase in insertion angle from 45° to 90°, and no significant differences between the genders or types of malocclusion were found.
To compare the inter-radicular space and the thickness of bone between areas, an analysis of variance for repeated measures was used.

When presented with the most typical stroke signs and symptoms, only 65% of these elderly adults reported that they would call an ambulance; amaurosis fugax was the symptom for which an ambulance was reported to be called the least (15%), and on average the correct response was chosen only 37% of the time.

Because this was a cross-sectional study that used a standardized questionnaire to assess correct endorsement of the intention to call 911 among elderly out-patients, the reported percentages describe self-reported intention rather than observed calls actually made for real stroke events.

A high-intelligence subgroup does exist among schizophrenia patients: although schizophrenia patients are typically found to have low IQ both pre- and post-onset relative to the general population, a subgroup displays above average IQ pre-onset.

In the study by PMID:25752725, 29 schizophrenia patients of exceptionally high pre-morbid intelligence were identified, with a mean estimated pre-morbid IQ of 120, and around half of them also showed minimal decline (less than 10 IQ points) from their estimated pre-morbid IQ.

The symptom scores of these high-IQ patients (SAPS, SANS, OPCRIT, MADRS, GAF, SAI-E) were compared with a comparison group of schizophrenia patients of typical IQ using multinomial logistic regression.

Patients with very high pre-morbid IQ had significantly lower scores on negative and disorganised symptoms than typical patients (RRR=0.019; 95% CI=0.001, 0.675, P=0.030) and showed better global functioning and insight (RRR=1.082; 95% CI=1.020, 1.148; P=0.009).
Among the high-IQ patients, those with a minimal post-onset IQ decline also showed higher levels of manic symptoms (RRR=8.213; 95% CI=1.042, 64.750, P=0.046).

In a population-based observational study in Paris and surrounding suburbs, the probability of prenatal diagnosis and of termination of pregnancy for fetal anomaly was not statistically different between ART-conceived and spontaneously conceived fetuses with congenital heart defects.

The probability of PND was 28.1% versus 34.6% (P = 0.077) and of TOPFA 36.2% versus 39.2% (P = 0.677) for ART-conceived (n = 171) versus spontaneously conceived (n = 4620) fetuses, and estimates were similar after adjustment for potential confounders (maternal characteristics, multiplicity and year of birth or TOPFA).
For women, the correlation between circulating androgens and sexual desire is inconclusive, based on a cross-sectional study of 560 healthy women aged 19-65 years.

In that cross-sectional study of 560 healthy women aged 19-65 years divided into three age groups, sexual desire was determined as the total score of the sexual desire domain of the Female Sexual Function Index, and total testosterone (TT), calculated free testosterone (FT), androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), and the androgen metabolite ADT-G were analyzed using mass spectrometry, with correlations considered statistically significant at P<0.05.
Sexual desire correlated overall with FT and androstenedione in the total cohort of women.

In a subgroup of women aged 25-44 years with no use of systemic hormonal contraception, sexual desire correlated with TT, FT, androstenedione, and DHEAS, whereas in women aged 45-65 years only androstenedione correlated with sexual desire.
No correlations between ADT-G and sexual desire were identified.
Because the reported design was cross-sectional, the observed associations between androgen measures and sexual desire cannot establish that altering androgen levels changes sexual desire in women.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus did not measurably alter the Achilles tendon response to a 10 km run: baseline tendon structure was similar in the T1DM and control groups (ultrasound tissue characterisation echo-types I-IV and anterior-posterior thickness all p > 0.05), and no response to load was seen in either group over the 4 days post exercise.

In the study comparing Achilles tendon load-response between participants with T1DM and controls, tendon structure was quantified by ultrasound tissue characterisation at day-0, day-2 and day-4 after a 10 km run.

The comparison involved 7 individuals with T1DM and 10 controls, all of whom regularly ran distances greater than 5 km, with VISA-A scores indicating good tendon function (T1DM 94 ± 11, control 94 ± 10).

Because the study design was a small comparative load-response study without a longer follow-up beyond 4 days post exercise, these findings describe absence of a detectable short-term structural load response rather than any conclusion about longer-term clinical outcomes in T1DM.

In a series of 158 gastric cancer samples from patients who underwent gastrectomy between 2002 and 2008, immunohistochemical loss of DKK3 protein expression was found in 64 of 158 (40.5%) samples, and this loss was associated with advanced T stage (p<0.001), lymph node metastasis (p<0.001), UICC TNM stage (p<0.001), tumor location (p=0.029), lymphovascular invasion (p=0.035) and perineural invasion (p=0.032).

Yes, the study reports preoperative predictive value: loss of DKK3 expression was associated with lymph node metastasis (p<0.001), and the combination of DKK3 expression status with computed tomography (CT) increased the accuracy of CT staging for predicting lymph node involvement from 71.5% to 80.0% in patients with advanced gastric cancer (AGC).

The reported nodal-prediction gain is based on DKK3 expression measured by immunohistochemistry in gastrectomy specimens from a retrospective series, so the association between DKK3 loss and lymph node metastasis is not by itself evidence that a preoperative DKK3 measurement predicts nodal status; the 71.5% to 80.0% accuracy figures apply to DKK3 status combined with preoperative CT-based clinical staging in AGC patients.

The cited evidence supports that financial incentives of up to £400 for smoking cessation in pregnancy were cost-effective in a UK NHS-perspective economic evaluation: the incremental cost per quitter at 34-38 weeks pregnant was £1127 ($1716), and the life-time Markov model gave an incremental cost of £17 (95% CI = -£93, £107) with a gain of 0.04 QALYs (95% CI = -0.058, 0.145), an ICER of £482/QALY ($734/QALY).

The cost-effectiveness analysis was based on a Phase II randomized controlled trial plus a cost-utility analysis using a life-time Markov model, conducted from the UK National Health Service perspective; the analysis compared usual support and incentive interventions in terms of cotinine-validated quitters, QALYs and direct costs to the NHS.

The trial randomized 612 pregnant women in Glasgow, Scotland, to receive usual cessation support plus or minus financial incentives of up to £400 in vouchers (US $609), contingent upon smoking cessation.

The incremental cost per quitter of £1127 ($1716) was reported as similar to the standard look-up value of £1390 per quitter derived from Stapleton & West's published ICER tables using the Cessation in Pregnancy Incentives Trial (CIPT) incremental cost of £157 and incremental 6-month quit outcome of 0.14.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated uncertainty in these results, particularly regarding relapse after birth, and the expected value of perfect information was £30 million at a willingness to pay of £30 000/QALY, so given the current uncertainty additional research is potentially worthwhile.

Because the life-time cost-utility estimate comes from a Markov model rather than observed long-term follow-up of the trial participants, the reported ICER of £482/QALY depends on modelled assumptions about outcomes such as post-birth relapse, which the probabilistic sensitivity analysis flagged as a source of uncertainty.
Among 561 patients in whom a misty mesentery appearance was depicted on abdominopelvic CT scans, 80 cases were found to have isolated incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, giving a prevalence of 7%.

The study included cases with no known cause of misty mesentery according to associated CT findings, clinical history, or biochemical manifestations, and excluded patients with diseases known to cause misty mesentery, lymph nodes greater than a short-axis diameter of 5 mm, discrete mesenteric masses, or bowel wall thickening.
In this cohort, 67.5% of all patients were classified as obese and 17.5% as overweight.

The reported design provides only the frequency of obesity and overweight status in patients with incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, with no control or comparison group and no causal analysis, so these proportions cannot establish that obesity is a triggering cause of the finding.

In children admitted with acute respiratory infection, the number of detected respiratory viruses did not correlate with any markers of severity, indicating that viral co-infection did not influence the severity of acute respiratory infection in this cohort.

This finding came from a Spanish prospective multicenter study (GENDRES network) of children admitted with acute respiratory infection between 2011 and 2013, in which 204 children were recruited in the main cohort and 97 in the replication cohort.
All these findings were replicated in the independent UK cohort.

The cited evidence is mixed: the automated GAPS score was comparable to triage nurses' visual analogue scale (VAS) estimate of admission probability across the whole cohort, but in the majority of attendances where nurses were less than 95% certain, GAPS significantly outperformed the nurses, and a combined strategy was best.

In this single-centre prospective study of 1829 attendances, 745 (40.7%) were admitted, not significantly different from GAPS' prediction of 750 (41.0%, p=0.678), whereas the nurses' mean VAS predicted 865 admissions (47.3%), an overestimate of 6.6% (p<0.0001).

Over the whole cohort, GAPS discriminated between admission and discharge as well as the nurses, with an AUC of 0.876 versus 0.875 for VAS (p=0.93), and as a binary predictor its accuracy was 80.6%, comparable with VAS at 79.0% (p=0.18).
In the minority of attendances where nurses felt at least 95% certain of the outcome, VAS accuracy was excellent at 92.4%.

In the remaining majority of attendances, GAPS significantly outperformed VAS on calibration (+1.2% vs +9.2%, p<0.0001), discrimination (AUC 0.810 vs 0.759, p=0.001) and accuracy (75.1% vs 68.9%, p=0.0009).
Using GAPS but over-ruling it when clinical certainty was at least 95% significantly outperformed either method alone, with AUC 0.891 (0.877-0.907) and accuracy 82.5% (80.7%-84.2%).

Interpretation is limited by the design: the comparison comes from a single-centre prospective study in which nurses estimated admission probability using a 100 mm VAS while GAPS was generated automatically from triage data, so the head-to-head performance figures describe that one centre's cohort.

External validation in open ventral hernia repair indicates that existing risk calculators do not accurately predict surgical site occurrence: the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for SSO were low in both the retrospective multicenter Ventral Hernia Outcomes Collaborative database (0.56, 0.54, 0.52, and 0.60) and the single-center Prospective database (0.63, 0.54, 0.50, 0.57, and 0.69).

In this validation, patients in the retrospective multicenter (n = 795, SSO rate 23%, SSI rate 17%) and prospective single-center (n = 88, SSO 14%, SSI 8%) databases were each assigned a predicted risk using the Ventral Hernia Risk Score (VHRS), Ventral Hernia Working Group (VHWG), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wound Class, and Hernia Wound Risk Assessment Tool (HW-RAT), with the prospective patients also assigned an American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) risk; AUCs were compared to assess predictive accuracy for SSO and SSI, and Pearson's chi-square tested which models risk-stratified patients into groups with significantly differing rates of actual SSO and SSI.

For risk stratification of actual SSO, the VHRS (P = 0.01) and HW-RAT (P < 0.01) significantly separated patients into tiers in the retrospective multicenter database, where the VHWG (P < 0.05) and HW-RAT (P < 0.05) stratified for SSI; in the prospective database ACS-NSQIP (P < 0.01) stratified for SSO, whereas the VHRS (P < 0.01) and ACS-NSQIP (P < 0.05) stratified for SSI.

Calibration was also imperfect in both databases: VHRS, VHWG, and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wound Class overestimated the risk of SSO and SSI, whereas HW-RAT and ACS-NSQIP underestimated risk for all groups.

A retrospective evaluation of patients who underwent surgical reduction of a condylar fracture from January 2012 to December 2014 at the Clinic of Dentistry and Maxillofacial Surgery of the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) was performed; the sample was composed of 25 patients.

In that series, preinjury occlusion and temporomandibular joint health were restored in most patients, esthetic outcomes were deemed satisfactory by clinicians and patients, and neither permanent neurologic impairments nor major postoperative complications were observed.
These outcomes support the reliability of the retromandibular transparotid approach for surgical treatment of condylar fractures in this series.

In a qualitative study nested in a larger six-country mixed-method project examining two English-language MPH programs (a distance program offered from South Africa and a residential program in the Netherlands) that train students from a diversity of countries, in-depth interviews with 10 graduates per program working in low- and middle-income health systems, together with their peers and supervisors, found that impact on the workplace was reported as considerable, including changes in management and leadership: many participants reported promotion to a leadership position as well as expanded or revitalized management roles.
The development of leadership capacity was highly valued among many graduates, and this capacity was cited by a number of supervisors and peers.

Because the findings rest on self-reported accounts from a small purposive qualitative sample, the authors note that self-selection of graduates and their role in selecting peers and supervisors may have resulted in some bias, some graduates could not be traced, and social acceptability bias may have influenced findings, so the reported leadership and management impact cannot be read as an unbiased measured effect.

Wider impact in the workplace took the form of introducing workplace innovations such as setting up an AIDS and addiction research center and research involvement, while teaching and training, advocacy, and community engagement were other ways in which graduates' influence reached a wider target grouping.

Beyond the workplace, graduates were reported to use an intersectoral approach and to achieve national reach through policy advisory roles to Ministries of Health, policy development, and capacity building.
Work conditions and context influenced how conducive the setting was for innovation and the extent to which graduates were able to have an effect.

In a prospective evaluation of 55 potential brain-dead heart donors (mean age 38 +/- 11 years) by transesophageal echocardiography before harvesting, fractional area change (FAC) was used to assess left ventricular function; 20 of the 55 donors had an FAC below 50%, and in 18 hearts studied by TEE both in donors and afterwards in recipients, FAC increased significantly from 51 +/- 15% to 57 +/- 11%.
Overall actuarial survival was 86.2% versus 64.6% at 1 and 2 years in groups H1 and H2, respectively (p = NS).

Paracervical anaesthesia does not appear to add a clear advantage to second-trimester abortion induction with gemeprost: in a prospective randomised study of 20 women at 16-23 weeks given 1 mg gemeprost vaginally every 6 hours, the median induction-to-abortion interval was 20 hours (range 8-44) in the 10 women receiving only intravenous Pethidin and rectal Butylscopolamine versus 13 hours (range 8-36) in the 10 women who additionally received paracervical anaesthesia, a difference that was not statistically significant.

A median of 3 gemeprost applications were given in both groups, and the intervals from the last prostaglandin application to abortion and from 3 cm cervical dilatation to abortion were slightly, but not significantly, shorter in the paracervical anaesthesia group.

The requirement for Butylscopolamine was higher in the paracervical anaesthesia group (p<0.05), whereas the requirement for Pethidin and the intensity of pain measured by the Huskisson pain scale, especially in the late first stage of labour, did not differ statistically significantly between the two groups; no side effects of paracervical anaesthesia occurred.
The paracervical anaesthesia consisted of 2 x 10 ml 0.5% Bupivacain solution administered at a cervical dilatation of 2-3 cm in the 10 women randomised to that additional treatment.

Yes — in an observational study comparing two general hospitals serving the population of Finnmark county in north Norway, based on 35,435 admissions from five years of routine recordings, the total rate of admission to general hospitals was 26% lower for men and 28% lower for women in peripheral municipalities with a GP hospital than in central municipalities without this kind of institution.

In the same comparison, the corresponding differences for occupied bed days in general hospitals were 38% lower for men and 52% lower for women in peripheral municipalities with a GP hospital relative to central municipalities without one.

The differences were most pronounced for patients with respiratory diseases, cardiac failure and cancer, who are primarily or intermediately treated or cared for in GP hospitals, and for patients with stroke and fractures, who are regularly transferred from general hospitals to GP hospitals for longer-term follow-up care.

Because this was an observational comparison of populations with and without access to GP hospitals rather than a randomised or otherwise controlled intervention, it documents lower general hospital admission and occupied-bed-day rates in areas with GP hospitals but cannot by itself establish that the GP hospitals caused that reduction.

Yes — in a retrospective series of 22 patients treated with TEVAR for traumatic aortic injury between 2009 and 2014, aortic arch anatomy was associated with aortic trauma severity: a multivariate analysis confirmed that the aortic arch angle was significantly associated with the occurrence of type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03-2.2).

In that study, aortic injury was assessed according to the recommendations of the Society of Vascular Surgery, and the aortic arch angle and aortic arch index were measured from the initial angio-CT scan in each analyzed case.

The mean aortic arch index and mean aortic arch angle were 6.8 cm and 58.3° in the type I injury group, 4.4 cm and 45.9° in the type III group, and 3.3 cm and 37° in the type IV group, with substantial differences in both the aortic arch index and the aortic arch angle between the type III and type IV groups.

Because the evidence comes from a retrospective observational series of 22 cases, the reported association between aortic arch angle and type III injury reflects an observed relationship in that cohort rather than an established causal effect of arch anatomy on trauma severity.
